description: AURALIS LAB is an R&D collective operating at the intersection of NASA spatial datasets, physical computing, and new media art. Our focus bridges high-precision hardware-software engineering with multisensory design. We approach the NASA Space Apps Challenge with technical rigor, structural efficiency, and artistic fidelity—engineering environments where complex scientific data transforms into immersive visual and spatial experiences.
summary: Welcome to SENSORA, where NASA data becomes something you play with your whole body. For the Earth Information Jukebox challenge, we didn’t just add a soundtrack to NASA visuals: we turned them into an instrument. Step in front of a wall-sized projection and a Kinect sensor reads your body. Raise a hand and the Earth turns. Spread your hands and you fly into a cloud of Saharan dust crossing the Atlantic; clap and you pull back to see the whole planet. Every aerosol has its own voice, so you hear smoke, dust, sea salt and volcanic sulfates as you explore them. Then leave the planet and raise both hands over images from the Webb and Hubble telescopes: every star your hands pass over becomes a note. Finally, walk from one side of the wall to the other across Landsat images, where green forests sing and dry land falls silent. No two visits sound the same, because you are the one composing. SENSORA turns NASA data into something you can see, hear and explore with your body, so science enthusiasts and people with visual, hearing or motor disabilities can all experience how our planet and universe change.
details:
AURALIS LAB’s Project Solution

SENSORA is an interactive audiovisual installation that turns NASA visualizations into music the audience creates with their bodies. A Kinect for Xbox 360 tracks one user without contact, and their movements control a wall projection and a soundscape generated in real time from the data itself. It is built around three experiences, Planet, Stars and Comparisons, that take visitors from Earth’s atmosphere to distant star clusters and back to the forests below.

How Does Our Solution Work

A visitor walks up to the wall and takes control of the whole experience. The Kinect captures color and depth, and Google’s MediaPipe Pose and Hand Landmarker models find their body and hands, while depth measures how close they are. Their movements become commands, and the data they explore becomes sound.

Experience 1 — Planet (Earth’s atmosphere, 2024)

The visitor stands in front of a 3D Earth wrapped with the 2,206 frames of NASA’s “Science On A Sphere: Aerosols in the Air,” built with the GEOS model of NASA’s Global Modeling and Assimilation Office. It shows how tiny particles moved around the globe from August 1 to September 14, 2024: Saharan dust crossing the Atlantic, sea salt spiraling around storms, smoke from wildfires in Canada and South America, and a sulfate plume from Hawaii’s Kīlauea volcano. To explore it, the visitor uses three gestures:

●      Drag: raise one hand and move it to rotate the planet.

●      Zoom: spread or close both hands.

●      Clap: zoom out to see the whole planet again.

Each aerosol type (dust, smoke/black carbon, sea salt or sulfates) has its own instrument, and its concentration changes the volume, pitch and rhythm, so visitors can hear a dust plume grow as they fly into it.

Experience 2 — Stars (Webb and Hubble)

Next, the visitor leaves Earth. The wall fills with images from the James Webb and Hubble space telescopes: the young star cluster Pismis 24, the star-forming region NGC 7129, the giant cloud Sagittarius B2 and the Cat’s Head Nebula. The visitor raises both hands and moves them across the sky; the Kinect measures their position and depth, and every star the hands pass over becomes a musical note. Move your hands and the melody changes. This experience builds on NASA’s own “Data Sonification: Caldwell 73,” which turns the stars of a cluster into music.

Experience 3 — Comparisons (Landsat, 2026)

Finally, the visitor returns to Earth’s surface. The visitor walks across the space from point A to point B, and a line follows their body over Landsat images from left to right. The land under the line sets the music: the greener the vegetation, the richer the nature soundscape; the drier the ground, the quieter it gets, down to silence. We use two NASA Earth Observatory images: the Coppermine River in Nunavut, Canada, seen by Landsat 9 on July 27 and September 6, 2026, when the green tundra turns red and orange; and Pennsylvania’s Pine Creek Gorge, seen by Landsat 8 on October 25, 2026, at peak fall color. By hearing the same place change between summer and fall, visitors learn how satellites track vegetation and the seasons.

In all three experiences the music is never a fixed track: it is always the data, played by the body of the person in front of the wall.

The installation benefits

science enthusiasts, students, museums and the wider community by:

●      Making NASA data accessible through three senses: sound for people who are blind or have low vision, visuals for people who are Deaf or hard of hearing, and touch-free gestures for people with limited mobility.

●      Turning complex Earth and space science into an experience people remember, not a chart they scroll past.

●      Using low-cost hardware (an Xbox 360 Kinect, a projector and speakers) and open-source software that schools and science fairs can reuse.

Our goal

To bring science enthusiasts and people with visual, hearing or motor disabilities closer to understanding scientific data through interaction. Although SENSORA explores three very different NASA datasets, it does not yet cover other Earth Information Center topics such as sea level, temperature or ice, which we would like to add next.

How it is creative

The audience’s body is the instrument. Instead of pressing play on a fixed soundtrack, each person composes the soundscape by moving through the data, so the same NASA visualization sounds different every time.

Factors we considered

●      Accessibility across visual, auditory and motor abilities.

●      Touch-free interaction, so nobody needs to hold a controller.

●      Scientific accuracy: the sound comes from the original NASA data, not from a pre-recorded track.

●      Cross-platform support for Linux (libfreenect) and Windows (Kinect SDK 1.8).

Tools and Technologies Used

Coding Languages:

●      Python → body tracking, gesture recognition and data streaming.

●      JavaScript → the 3D globe (three.js) and sound synthesis (Tone.js).

Body Tracking:

●      Kinect for Xbox 360 + libfreenect → color and depth capture on Linux (Kinect SDK 1.8 on Windows).

●      Google MediaPipe Pose and Hand Landmarker → body and hand detection of the user.

●      OpenCV and NumPy → image processing.

Visuals (VISORA module):

●      three.js → interactive 3D globe textured with NASA frames.

●      TouchDesigner → real-time visuals.

●      MapMap → projection mapping onto the wall.

Sound (SONORA module):

●      Tone.js → real-time synthesis.

●      python-osc → sends body data to TouchDesigner over OSC.

Hardware:

●      Kinect for Xbox 360 with a custom case, projector, speakers and computer.
